statement: Cubes stand on a 2 by 2 square. The front view shows heights 3 (left) and 1 (right). The side view shows 3 (front) and 2 (back). What is the largest possible number of cubes?

choices.misconception: I added the heights in the front view, $3 + 1 = 4$, as if the front view shows every cube.
I added the heights in the side view, $3 + 2 = 5$, as if the side view shows every cube.
I put no cubes on the back right square, but 1 cube fits there without changing either view.
I added the front view and the side view together, $4 + 5 = 9$, but those views show some of the same cubes.

hints: Draw the 2 by 2 square from above and give each place a height.
Each stack is limited twice: by its half in the front view and by its row in the side view. For the most cubes, make every stack as tall as both limits allow.
The stack at front left can be 3 tall, at back left 2, at front right 1, at back right 1.

solutions.reliable: Call the four places front left, back left, front right, back right. A stack can be no taller than its half in the front view and no taller than its row in the side view. Front left: at most 3 and at most 3, so 3. Back left: at most 3 and at most 2, so 2. Front right: at most 1 and at most 3, so 1. Back right: at most 1 and at most 2, so 1. These heights do give exactly the two views, so the largest number is $3 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7$. The transferable idea: each view gives an upper limit, so the largest building takes the smaller limit for every stack.

whyOnTest: Combining two views into a plan of heights, and seeing that views limit but do not fix the count, is the key idea of view problems.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
